stimulus_title: The Night Shift at the Seed Library
stimulus_text:
For eleven years the seed library in Barangay Masagana opened only on Saturday mornings, and for eleven years it served the same forty households. Then a retired agriculturist named Delia proposed something the committee found faintly absurd: open it at night.

Her reasoning was unglamorous. The farmers who most needed drought-tolerant seed were the ones least able to collect it, because Saturday morning was market morning, and market morning was the only income some of them had. A library that opened when its users were busy was, she argued, a library that had quietly chosen its easiest patrons.

The committee resisted, though not on the merits. There was no budget for lighting. No one wanted to staff a counter at nine in the evening. And besides, attendance had been stable for a decade, which the committee read as success and Delia read as a ceiling.

She won the argument by narrowing it. Not a new programme, she said, but six Thursdays. Borrow the lamps. She would take the counter herself.

By the fourth Thursday the register listed ninety-three households. More interesting than the number was its composition: two thirds of the new borrowers had never set foot in the building, and most asked for varieties the Saturday collection had never stocked, because nobody had ever thought to ask them what they planted. The committee approved the night shift permanently that December, and recorded the decision as an expansion of service hours.

Delia, in her own notes, recorded it differently. The library had not been short of seed, she wrote. It had been short of the people who would have told it what was missing.
